Philadelphia has had an open window throughout this decade, as Harper won his second MVP in 2021. But they lost the World Series in 2022 and have gone backward since then, losing in the 2023 NLCS, the 2024 and 2025 NLDS and the Wild Card this year.

articles.title: Washington girls walk off cross country meet in protest of male athlete, parents reveal how it came to this
articles.excerpt:
Washington state parents Kevin and Sarah Burns watched their daughter Holly Burns join a mass protest of female athletes who walked off a cross country meet in response to a male competitor.

Holly Bu...
articles.body_text:
Washington state parents Kevin and Sarah Burns watched their daughter Holly Burns join a mass protest of female athletes who walked off a cross country meet in response to a male competitor.

Holly Burns and about a dozen other girls walked away from a cross-country race in Washington on Tuesday.

They refused to compete against a male athlete who had started the season racing on the boys’ team.

When the race began, half of the girls competing, and the male athlete, took off running.

Burns and the other half of the girls slowly walked forward past the starting line, and then into the nearby tree line, sacrificing one of their high school competitions.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Footage of the protest has since gone viral across social media, igniting widespread awareness for one of the trans athlete incidents currently plaguing Washington state.

For Burns, a Camas High School runner, the decision to protest was reinforced by strength in numbers. Her parents, Kevin and Sarah Burns, told OutKick their daughter initially wanted to avoid "making waves."

"She wanted to kind of play it safe, so we, we weren't going to push it. We just kind of let her kind of feel it out. We told her that. We supported her whichever decision she tries to make," Kevins said.

DAD BANNED FROM SCHOOL GROUNDS AFTER PROTESTING TRANS RUNNER COMPETING AGAINST HIS DAUGHTER

The girls shared their concerns. They decided to act together. And her parents backed her.

"The more I heard about her friends wanting to do something, the more I heard about her team wanting to do something, we definitely were in support of that," Kevin said.

"We told her, do what you think is best."

The Oct. 13 meet pitted Camas against Battle Ground. Camas hosted the event at the Underwriters Lab campus, where the girls’ race was scheduled for 4 p.m.

The Burnses said they learned about the athlete’s move to girls’ competition recently. They worried about what it would mean for their daughter and her teammates.

"You hear about it, but you just never think it’s going to be on your kid’s small cross-country team," Sarah said.

ATTORNEY FOR ALLEGED VICTIM OF TRANS ATHLETE SEXUAL ASSAULT SAYS SCOTUS FIGHT CAN HELP SET TITLE IX PRECEDENT

A Camas High cross country runner, who switched from the boys team to the girls team midseason, stands at the start line of a girls race in at the Nike Hole in the Wall XC Invitational. (OutKick)

Camas School District has said it follows Washington law and Washington Interscholastic Activities Association eligibility rules.

For the Burnses, that policy leaves their daughter’s concerns unresolved.

"I don’t see how it’s OK to discriminate against my daughter and the daughters of everyone else that is trying to fairly compete," Kevin said.

Their own protest began before the girls walked off.

FEMALE ATHLETES, WOMEN'S SPORTS ADVOCATES SPEAK ON CAPITOL HILL AS TRANS ATHLETE ISSUE HOVERS OVER MIDTERMS

They arrived with signs, and security challenged them, the parents said.

"They said that we’re not allowed to hold up signs at this event today," Kevin Burns said. "I questioned them if that was constitutionally legal, if we could express ourselves by just holding a sign. And we kind of went back and forth about public versus private property. And in the end, it didn’t seem like they really had a grasp on what they could tell us to do or not.

"So I just went ahead and held up my sign, and they had several security guards following me and pestering me and telling me that I would have to leave. And I just said, no, I’m not going to leave."

A Camas High cross country runner, who switched from the boys team to the girls team midseason, stands at the start line of a girls race in at the Nike Hole in the Wall XC Invitational. (OutKick)

Other parents approached, they said. Some offered support. Others said they agreed but feared the backlash that could follow speaking publicly.

At one point, Sarah said she had a confrontation with a woman who identified herself as a psychiatric nurse.

"I had a lady that came up to me and said she was a psychiatric nurse and that I was a disgusting human for holding up this sign and that I was doing psychological damage to these children," Sarah said. "I told her that one day I’m gonna have to stand before my Lord and Savior and I’m gonna feel good about this."

The Burnses said they respected the girls who chose to race Tuesday. They believed some wanted to preserve their chances of competing in postseason meets.

"I think they all have to make their own decision," they said.

For Holly, they do not yet know what sitting out will mean.

"Well, we don’t know that yet," they said when asked whether the protest cost her a chance at something she had worked toward.

"But there’s cost to everything when you stand up for what you believe is right, I think. If there wasn’t, then you’re not really standing up for anything," they said.

"Her goal this season was just to have fun and compete and do the best that she could."

Now her parents hope she can keep pursuing those goals while standing alongside her teammates.

More races remain. Camas lists its next championship meet for Oct. 21 at Lewisville Regional Park.

Another decision awaits Washington voters on Nov. 3.

Initiative 638 would prohibit students it defines as biologically male from competing in certain female-only interschool athletic competitions. It would require students seeking to enter those competitions to provide verification of biological sex from a healthcare provider.

But even if voters approve it, the measure would take effect 30 days after the election. Washington’s state cross-country championships are scheduled for Nov. 7.

The athlete at the center of the dispute had already competed in several girls’ races.

On Sept. 5, the runner finished 76th in a boys’ junior varsity race at the Ultimook meet in Oregon.

(From left to right) Female athletes Frances Staudt, Bailey Andersen, Sadie Sullivan, Kendall Kotzmacher and Alanna Smith stand behind emcee and podcast host Brandi Kruse at a Protecting Fairness in Girls' Sports rally in Vancouver, Washington. (Derek Shook for OutKick)

By Sept. 15, the runner was competing in the girls’ race at a Camas meet involving Skyview.

The Burnses had not spoken with the athlete or the athlete’s family.

Their position, they said, was that the runner should compete with boys.

"Their child has every right to participate in the boys athletics, just like they did at the beginning of the season, but it’s not fair to the girls," they said during the interview.

Holly’s parents rejected the idea that the stakes become insignificant because the athletes are in high school.

"Some of these girls work really hard to compete. It’s most of what they do all summer long. It means a lot to them," they said.

They argued that losing opportunities can undo the rewards of that effort.

"Then that’s devastating to all the hard work. It erases everything they’ve done."

The dispute unfolds against a broader conflict over Washington’s eligibility policies.

President Donald Trump’s Feb. 5, 2025, executive order directed federal agencies to protect female athletic opportunities and prioritize Title IX enforcement against federally funded institutions that require female athletes to compete against males in women’s categories.

Federal officials opened an investigation into Washington’s Office of Superintendent of Public Instruction in April 2025.

State Superintendent Chris Reykdal defended Washington’s protections. He said the state had allowed students to participate in athletics consistent with their gender identity since 2007 and would continue enforcing its laws unless Congress or federal courts changed the legal requirements.

A separate Washington sports dispute has also reached the Supreme Court.

A high school wrestler identified in court filings as K.M.K. and her mother, Stephanie Brown, have requested emergency relief, including notice and an opportunity to decline competition against male athletes without penalties.

The WIAA opposed the application in a filing Tuesday, arguing that the requested relief would conflict with state law and compromise other students’ privacy. The Supreme Court’s docket showed the responses filed Tuesday and no ruling on the application.

"So we made a few contacts and we might go forward with that and have a more organized protest the next time," Kevin said.

Asked whether they would return with more signs and shirts, the answer came quickly.

They also said they were prepared for greater national attention if it helped bring change.

Some friends disagree with their position. The couple hopes those relationships can survive the dispute.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"I think we can respect each other outside of the controversy," they said.

Their fears extend beyond one race. They worry about what the policy means for college athletics, Olympic competition and other spaces reserved for women.

"Women’s spaces will be erased," they said.

For now, their daughter has chosen to stand with her teammates.

Her parents want other families to know they can speak up, too.

"Girls need their own space. They need their sports. They need their athletics."

OutKick reached out to Camas, WIAA, Washington Superintendent for Public Instruction and Battle Ground for comment. Battle Ground hosted the race.

Jackson Thompson is a sports reporter for Fox News Digital covering critical political and cultural issues in sports, with an investigative lens. Jackson's reporting has been cited in federal government actions related to the enforcement of Title IX, and in legacy media outlets including The New York Times, The Los Angeles Times, The Philadelphia Inquirer, The Associated Press and ESPN.com.

articles.title: Trump heads to rallies in Arizona and Montana after campaign stop-off in Alaska – US politics live
articles.excerpt:
Trump has taken to campaigning in conservative-leaning ​parts of competitive states, rather than in more politically diverse areas

The family of a British man who was killed by a tiger at a wildlife ...
articles.body_text:
Trump has taken to campaigning in conservative-leaning ​parts of competitive states, rather than in more politically diverse areas

The family of a British man who was killed by a tiger at a wildlife park have spoken of their “severe distress” after Donald Trump shared a video of the incident on social media.

The president posted footage of William Chapman, 23, being fatally attacked by a tiger at the Yorkshire Wildlife Park to 13m followers on his Truth Social platform on Tuesday evening.

Trump accompanied the short clip – which showed the animal biting and clawing Chapman as he sat in the enclosure, but not him being killed – with the signed message: “Don’t ever mess with nature!”

On Wednesday morning Trump followed this up with another post – this time an AI-generated video of him grappling with a tiger, which appears to mimic the original.

The clip, which is accompanied by the song ‘The Lion Sleeps Tonight’, features the president copying the pointing gesture made by Chapman and ends with him hugging the animal.

Chapman’s family said in a statement that “deeply offensive media content is causing them severe distress”.

They also posted a tribute describing him as a “bright, warm and engaging young man” and questioning what part his “significant mental illness over a number of years” and prescribed strong medication played in the incident.

Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

Donald Trump will attend campaign rallies in Arizona and Montana later today, having spent the past 24 hours in Alaska – a sign of his party’s recent polling woes.

Conservative Alaska is one of several where the Democrats have a chance of flipping a Senate seat amid voter dissatisfaction with the cost of living and the Iran war.

Polling has shown Democratic candidate Mary Peltola tied ⁠or slightly ahead of incumbent Republican senator Dan ⁠Sullivan in a state the president carried by 14 percentage points in 2024.

Here, as in much of the United States, the president’s approval rating is flopping, hit by rising diesel and gasoline prices and a conflict in the Middle East that has proven deeply unpopular with voters.

Opening for Trump, Sullivan acknowledged that Alaskans face “challenges” when it comes to energy costs. But “the conflict in the Middle East is temporary,” he said. “The true forever war is the national Democrats’ war against Alaska oil and gas ⁠and our jobs.“

The president has taken to campaigning in conservative-leaning ​parts of competitive states, rather than in more politically diverse areas with more votes potentially up for grabs.

At one point, Trump pardoned two local repair shop owners who were convicted of violating the federal Clean Air Act for removing pollution controls on diesel engines.

He also encouraged Republicans to vote by mail – a process he has repeatedly sought to curtail and discredit. Trump will spend Wednesday campaigning in Arizona and Montana.

In Alaska, Donald Trump repeated his false claim that he had to start his war on Iran because, “they were two weeks away from having a nuclear weapon”. In fact, US intelligence agencies reported to Congress in 2025 that Iran had suspended its pursuit of nuclear weapons in 2003. Despite that assessment, in the summer of 2025, Trump ordered the US bombing of Iran’s nuclear enrichment facilities which he later claimed had “obliterated” the country’s nuclear program. Eight months after that, he launched a full-scale war on Iran justified, he now says, by Iran being just weeks away from getting the bomb.

Aboard Air Force One on his way to Alaska for a campaign rally, the president of the United States posted video of a British man who was fatally mauled by a tiger last week on his social media platform with the mocking caption: “Don’t ever mess with nature!”

The new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, passed on an opportunity to set the record straight on whether she is licensed to practice law anywhere in the United States. Asked “Where did you pass the bar exam?” Zacharia just said: “I moved to China.”

articles.title: Russell Brand was ‘ruthless and calculated’, prosecutors tell jury as rape and sexual assault trial begins – live
articles.excerpt:
Russell Brand back in Southwark crown court today where his rape and sexual assault trial begins

Karmy-Jones said the allegations “punctuate” 10 years of Brand’s life when “his career was beginning t...
articles.body_text:
Russell Brand back in Southwark crown court today where his rape and sexual assault trial begins

Karmy-Jones said the allegations “punctuate” 10 years of Brand’s life when “his career was beginning to flourish”.

“His public profile was taking off as he was progressing from doing gigs as a standup comedian at pubs and clubs to a TV presenter, an actor and Hollywood movie star,” she told jurors.

She added that the circumstances of the alleged offences were “as wide and as varied as the defendant’s career”, and that the offending took place in a number of locations including a hotel room, workplaces, a toilet cubicle in a bar and at his home address.

Continuing her opening statement, Karmy-Jones said:

double quotation markSome of the women involved protested and said no, others had no opportunity to react to his advances but it mattered not to the defendant.

Regardless of who they were and what they said or did, Russell Brand was not deterred.

His desire, strong desire for some form of sexual contact, was indiscriminate and voracious. He would be nice when he wanted to be, funny – undoubtedly – charming, likable even – when he wanted something in return – but then demanding, entitled, a flirt with a huge sexual appetite, childlike in his expectation that his every desire should be met.

He was ruthless, calculated and manipulative, and, the prosecution say, a sexual predator.”

Taking jurors through the third allegation, Karmy-Jones said Brand pulled another woman into a toilet during an incident at a bar in Soho in 2004.

The third complainant was “not so lucky as to be able to pull away”, the prosecutor said.

The court heard Brand “grabbed her arm and held her quite strongly and pulled her into the lavatory” where he allegedly orally raped her.

Karmy-Jones told jurors that the woman said “what are you doing – I don’t want to do this” to which Brand replied “‘Oh come on don’t be a spoil sport, you want to’ or something along those lines”.

The prosecution outlined the second allegation against Brand, involving a woman who worked at MTV at the time of the alleged incident in 2001.

The court heard that the woman offered to show Brand where the toilets were, when he allegedly told her “come in, go on, come in” and “grabbed her hard by her forearm”.

Karmy-Jones told jurors the alleged victim “resisted by struggling and pulling back”.

double quotation markShe continued to resist saying ‘I’m not coming in there, don’t be silly, are you mad – get off’, and she managed to pull herself away, and to release his grasp.

At that point he gave up and went into the toilet, and she left the area.”

The woman felt “bewildered and shocked” by the alleged assault, jurors were told.

Continuing with the first alleged victim, Karmy-Jones said the woman met Brand at a fringe event at the Labour party conference where he was performing, and that they had engaged in a conversation that later continued in a hotel room.

The complainant, who was in her 20s at the time, said when she came out of the bathroom at her hotel room, Brand was topless, the court heard.

double quotation markAs she came out of the bathroom he was prancing around the room – a bit like an ostrich, doing silly walks like Basil Fawlty, she said.

She was taken aback, she was shocked, she didn’t really know what to do – and in her words she froze.

She asked him why he had taken his clothes off, and he said something along the lines of – ‘It’s okay, it’s just how I am, don’t worry…. I’m mostly naked at home’.”

The court heard how Brand allegedly raped the woman, who said she was “drifting out of her head” during the alleged attack, and that he later “behaved as if nothing had happened”.

Karmy-Jones said the alleged victim was “left in shock”, “crying” and feeling “ashamed”, “dirty” and “stupid”.

She added: “Throughout she felt it was her fault, she almost chastised herself for inviting him back to her room.”

Karmy-Jones turned to the first allegation against Brand, in which he is alleged to have raped a woman in a hotel room during a Labour party conference in Bournemouth in 1999.

She told the court a witness named Mark Pinheiro said he recalled that Brand was “desperate” to have sex before they left the conference.

double quotation markAs you will hear, the defendant did achieve his objective.

He found a victim, engaged with her, told her ‘exactly what she needed to hear’, and then manipulated the situation so as to have sex with her.”

The court heard Brand had burst into a flat the morning after the alleged rape in Bournemouth and told the group he was with to “pack up their stuff” and that they “had to leave town immediately”. Karmy-Jones said:

double quotation markOnce in the car, the defendant behaved oddly, shrinking down in the back seat to hide his head beneath the window.

When pressed about where he had been the night before, and why they had to leave so abruptly, he said he had forgotten he had an audition.”

Brand would later admit to Pinheiro that it was not an audition but that he had had sex with a woman in Bournemouth the night before their hasty departure, telling him that things “might have got a little out of hand”, Karmy-Jones told jurors.

The prosecution cited remarks made by Brand’s friends during the early years of his career, including one who described the comedian as someone who “was rampant in his desire to have sex”.

Another friend, speaking about Brand before he found fame, described him as “very impulsive. His impulsivity led him to be very single-minded, and women and sex were a goal and an obsession,” Karmy-Jones told the court.

She told jurors that these comments would provide an insight into what Brand was like in his former years.

She said: “This is important because what you must bear in mind in this case is that, although you’re sat as jurors in Southwark crown court on October 14 2026 listening to my opening address, you will be considering offences that took place between around 27 and 17 years ago, when the defendant was aged roughly between 24-33.

“So the man who you will be considering in this trial is not the Mr Brand who is sitting in the dock, who is now 51.”

She added that while Brand may have changed both physically and as a person in the years since that “his responsibility for wrongs done, crimes committed at a younger age remain the same”.

Karmy-Jones said the allegations “punctuate” 10 years of Brand’s life when “his career was beginning to flourish”.

“His public profile was taking off as he was progressing from doing gigs as a standup comedian at pubs and clubs to a TV presenter, an actor and Hollywood movie star,” she told jurors.

She added that the circumstances of the alleged offences were “as wide and as varied as the defendant’s career”, and that the offending took place in a number of locations including a hotel room, workplaces, a toilet cubicle in a bar and at his home address.

Continuing her opening statement, Karmy-Jones said:

double quotation markSome of the women involved protested and said no, others had no opportunity to react to his advances but it mattered not to the defendant.

Regardless of who they were and what they said or did, Russell Brand was not deterred.

His desire, strong desire for some form of sexual contact, was indiscriminate and voracious. He would be nice when he wanted to be, funny – undoubtedly – charming, likable even – when he wanted something in return – but then demanding, entitled, a flirt with a huge sexual appetite, childlike in his expectation that his every desire should be met.

He was ruthless, calculated and manipulative, and, the prosecution say, a sexual predator.”

Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones has begun proceedings by outlining the charges against Russell Brand to the court.

double quotation markRussell Brand, as you may know, and if you didn’t know before this trial, is a celebrity.

He was born on June 4 1975 making him now 51 years old.

He is here as he has been charged with a number of sexual offences including rape and sexual assault as you heard, those offences were committed against six different women between approximately 1999 and 2009.

Six different women, six women who did not know each other then and do not know each other now, who have never met each other, and who came forward independently of each other.

Their paths all crossed the defendant’s either through their employment, social events or through attending gigs where he was performing.”

Brand was driven to the court in a black Mercedes-Benz van, which parked directly outside the court building, where crowds of reporters and photographers had gathered for his trial.

Brand waited inside the vehicle for around a minute before stepping out, wearing a dark suit, a black-and-white striped shirt, a long white tie and sunglasses. He reached out for his wife’s hand before the pair walked together towards the court.

Russell Brand spoke to the media as he arrived at court this morning, saying he was feeling “concerned but hopeful”.

He said: “Today I feel blessed, I feel of course concerned but hopeful that this process will lead to good outcomes for everybody involved.

Russell Brand will be back in Southwark crown court today where his rape and sexual assault trial is expected to begin.

We should be hearing opening statements from the prosecution, which will set out an overview of the allegations against the 51-year-old comedian. He has been charged with three counts of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women, in allegations that date from 1999 to 2009. Brand has pleaded not guilty to all the charges.

He has been pictured arriving at court this morning with his wife, Laura Gallacher.

A jury was sworn in yesterday, with a warning from the judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, to ignore past reporting about Brand and allegations of sexual misconduct. You can read our report here:

The Press Association has been outside court this morning, where news crews have been setting up shop several hours before the trial begins. Here’s what the news agency reports:

double quotation markA crowd of members of the press were gathered outside Southwark crown court hours before Russell Brand’s trial was due to start.

Photographers, video journalists and news presenters could be seen in position at around 7.30am, while a line of reporters waited to get in to the court building.

Members of court security were also outside the building, along with a small group of police officers.

One police officer was heard telling members of the press to stay behind barriers which were in place directly outside the building.”

The trial is scheduled to begin at 10am, so follow along for live updates throughout the day as the case gets under way.

articles.title: Badenoch and Farage in spat over Chagos Islands, as she calls his offer to Trump ‘humiliating’ – UK politics live
articles.excerpt:
Prime minister will face questions from leader of the opposition and other MPs

Barack Obama, the former US president, delivered a message about hope on a visit to Northern Ireland yesterday. He urged...
articles.body_text:
Prime minister will face questions from leader of the opposition and other MPs

Barack Obama, the former US president, delivered a message about hope on a visit to Northern Ireland yesterday. He urged people to “insist that we can do better than we’re doing right now”.

He was in Belfast to accept an honorary degree, and at a Q&A event later he was asked what hope meant to him.

He said people had to “rediscover what’s the story we tell about how we’re going to live together, and see each other, and recognise each other, and disagree, and yet, still care for each other”. He went on:

double quotation markThe Good Friday agreement came about not just because of exhaustion and people being weary of violence. It was also – somebody started imagining something better, and they saw themselves and each other in a different kind of way.

People ask me sometimes how I can still be hopeful. It’s an assertion. It’s a practice. It is me saying: this is how I prefer to live.

I am going to assume the best in people. I am going to be willing to recognise my own flaws and consider how I can be better.

I’m going to insist that we can do better than we’re doing right now.

And there’s something in us that recognises ourselves and others, that has an impulse towards kindness, but also an impulse towards cruelty, and I know which side of that contest I want to be on. And I will fight for that, even if I don’t always think it’s going to win.

Earlier, at the degree ceremony at Queen’s University Belfast, Obama said:

double quotation markThe Good Friday agreement is still a shining example of what can happen when people put aside old wounds and choose peace.

But as we have seen in many countries, including in my home country the United States, peace and democracy are not inevitable. They have to be chosen, again and again.

Charities and volunteers who help asylum seekers get to the UK should face potential criminal prosecution, Nigel Farage has said in an interview with a rightwing US podcaster. Peter Walker has the story.

This is not the first time Reform UK has proposed this idea. Zia Yusuf, the party’s home affairs spokesperson, says he would call this “Polanski’s law” because Zack Polanski, the Green party leader, is a proud supporter of the rights of asylum seekers.

There was a further example of Tory willingness to criticise Donald Trump (see 10.01am) on Sky News this morning. Kevin Hollinrake, the Conservative chair, said he was “massively worried” about the US seeming to soften its attitude towards Russia. “We’ve got to stand shoulder to shoulder with [President] Zelenskyy,” he said.

As my colleague Peter Walker predicted, the Lib Dem MPs’ ‘crisis meeting’ about the future of Ed Davey as leader last night went nowhwere in the end. Chris Mason from the BBC has a good story about it here. Here’s an extract.

double quotation markThe Liberal Democrat leader arrived smiling, flanked by several loyal MPs, but made no comment as he entered the room.

Nearly four hours later, when the meeting broke up, his deputy Daisy Cooper said: “There is overwhelming support for Ed in the parliamentary party and a real sense that we need to come together as a group.”

Earlier, behind closed doors, we understand Sir Ed told his MPs: “We have made changes. I am happy to embrace more changes. I want us to work as a united front.” Another tacit nod to things being less than united recently.

The Lib Dem MP Bobby Dean has been giving interviews this morning. He told Sky News that the meeting was “mostly it was a show of strength for Ed, really, a lot of people behind [him]. I know that there were some individuals that came out [to criticise Davey] in the last week, but it really isn’t the group feeling.”

Here are more comments from Kemi Badenoch on what Nigel Farage told a US podcast about wanting to make an offer to President Trump in relation to the Chagos Islands. (See 9.56am.)

double quotation markIt is mad for someone who wants to be prime minister to say we should give away one piece of British territory just to stop an American President talking about another …

Nigel Farage has made such a huge fuss about defending the Chagos Islands. He calls this making a deal. Giving away British territory in return for someone keeping quiet is not a deal. It is humiliating.

While in some respects the Nigel Farage/Kemi Badenoch Chagos Islands row (see 9.56am) is just a slightly manufactured spat between two leaders who are not in a position to decide the future of the Chagos Islands anyway, it is revealing about the state of opposition politics, in three respects.

First, this is further evidence that the fight between the Tories and Reform UK is increasingly bitter. Here they are arguing over a policy where, essentially, their views are very similar. This time last year there was informal talk of a potential pact. Now there is an acrimonious fight to be the dominant party on the right.

Second, it is interesting that Badenoch keen to attack Farage on the grounds of his closeness to Donald Trump. Two years ago, Badenoch found it hard to say a bad word about the US president. But, as Trump gets every more erratic and unpopular, Badenoch is increasingly willing to say he’s wrong – and having him as a friend becomes ever more of a problem for the Reform UK leader.

And, third, this is further evidence that papers like the Telegraph, the Daily Mail and the Sun, which until recently were probably more pro-Farage than pro-Conservative, and now siding more with Badenoch’s party. (Farage was complaining about this at his press conference on Monday.)

While Andy Burnham prepares for PMQs, he may be amused by a peculiar row that has broken out between Nigel Farage and Kemi Badenoch, the leaders of the two most prominent rightwing opposition parties. It is about the Chagos Islands – a subject on which until recently the Tories and Reform UK were united in their opposition to Labour’s proposed deal transferring sovereignty to Mauritius.

The Telegraph has a story by Genevieve Holl-Allen quoting what Farage, the Reform UK leader, recently told a US podcast. He said he would have handed it over to President Trump. Farage said:

double quotation markI’d have gone in and said, ‘Right, you know what, mate? Chagos, it’s yours. Diego Garcia, in perpetuity, the most strategic American military base in the world, which it is.

Outside mainland America, Diego is the most important thing America has for nuclear subs, for long-range bombers, for all of it.

I’d have said, ‘Right, I’m guaranteeing you that. I’m giving up on this surrender. In return, just please stop talking about the Falkland Islands. I know you like [Argentina’s president Javier] Milei, but this really matters to us’. And there’s a trade, you see.

I give him something. I ask for something back. He’d get that. He’d understand that. He’s a businessman. He’s a trader.

The Telegraph put these remarks to Badenoch, and its story leads off on her reaction. The Tory leader said:

double quotation markGiving away British territory in return for someone keeping quiet is not a deal. It is humiliating.

There is no pride in our country in the way he talks about us. This is careless, loose talk from a man who wants to be responsible for Britain’s national security.

The Chagos Islands are British. And the Falklands are British and will remain British, irrespective of what the American president says. When Donald Trump is right, we should say so. When he is wrong, we should have the confidence to tell him.

Last night Farage hit back, claiming the Telegraph, and Badenoch, had misinterpreted what he had said. He was not really talking about giving the US the whole of the Chagos Islands, he said; he was just proposing guaranteed use of the Diego Garcia military base in perpetuity (which is close to what Labour is offering the US anyway). Farage said:

double quotation markThis is totally dishonest journalism. I make it clear that I am opposed to the surrender of sovereignty to Mauritius. I would offer the use of Diego Garcia to the USA in perpetuity. In return I would want America to go quiet on the Falklands.

No one has fought harder to save the Chagos Islands from being given away than I have, unlike the Tories and Labour trying to give them away. I have even helped repopulate the islands with Chagossians.

Good morning. Andy Burnham is taking PMQs this afternoon, but he will regard his most important engagement as the meeting he has with Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the Ukrainian president, later in No 10. Peter Walker has a preview.

When Keir Starmer talked about his best achievements as PM, he said one of the things he was most proud of was being able to embrace Zelenskyy outside No 10 only 24 hours after President Trump humiliated him in the Oval Office, in what was a moving and unequivocal show of British support for Ukraine at a moment of peril. The circumstances are not exactly the same today, but Trump called for Zelenskyy to be replaced at the weekend, and – again – Burnham is signalling that, if Ukraine cannot always rely on Washington, it can rely on London.

double quotation markOur rock-solid support to Ukraine is vital for keeping us safe here in the UK and ensuring those on the frontlines have the equipment they need to push back Russia.

My message to the Ukrainian people could not be clearer, we are with you for as long as it takes, and we will go further and faster in our support to back your courageous fight for peace in Europe.

It is not just the right thing to do, but it’s the necessary thing to do. Russia’s aggression cannot be allowed to succeed on our continent.

Burnham is also announcing that the UK will “accelerate deliveries of British Lightweight Multirole Missiles (LMMs), which have proven extremely effective against jet-powered drones that are being used to strike far beyond the front lines in Ukraine, including Kyiv and beyond.” No 10 says:

double quotation markThe [Russian] drones are faster and can fly far higher than propeller-driven Shaheds, making them harder to detect and destroy before they hit targets.

The UK has already committed £1.6 billion to deliver more than 5,000 LMMs to Ukraine over the next four years and will accelerate £10m of the £45m package of missiles announced today to meet Ukraine’s most urgent winter requirements.

10.30am: Dominic Cummings, Boris Johnson’s former chief adviser, gives evidence to the Lords constitution committee on constitutional safeguards.

Noon: Andy Burnham faces Kemi Badenoch at PMQs.

After 12.30pm: MPs debate a Tory opposition day motion saying that the government should not place asylum seekers in a military camp near Piddington, and that it should “withdraw from the European convention on human rights in order to deport illegal migrants”.

Afternoon: Burnham hosts Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the Ukrainian president, in Downing Street.

3pm: Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, gives evidence to the Commons energy committee.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

articles.title: Bipartisan senators demand Trump scrap Russia diesel deal, call it 'betrayal' of US allies
articles.excerpt:
President Donald Trump speaks about intel sharing with Ukraine and a diesel deal with Russia during the U.S. war against Iran.

A bipartisan group of senators is urging Donald Trump to scrap his recen...
articles.body_text:
President Donald Trump speaks about intel sharing with Ukraine and a diesel deal with Russia during the U.S. war against Iran.

A bipartisan group of senators is urging Donald Trump to scrap his recently announced diesel deal with Russia, warning it could help President Vladimir Putin finance his war against Ukraine and calling the agreement "a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our Allies."

"The Treasury Department’s General License No. 135, which lifts sanctions on Russia’s diesel exports, only provides Putin with more fuel to finance his war machine and enables Russia to continue its brutal attacks on Ukrainian civilians. Granting Moscow the ability to sell Russian diesel freely in global markets damages American security interests and is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine, who continue to defend themselves from Putin’s murderous, illegal war. This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our Allies; it should be rescinded," the senators asserted in the missive.

The letter, which also includes a note of cc to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, is signed by GOP Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina, Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, Susan Collins of Maine, Alan Stuart Armstrong of Oklahoma, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, and John Cornyn of Texas, as well as Democratic Sens. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, Dick Durbin of Illinois, Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, Jack Reed of Rhode Island, and Chris Coons of Delaware.

REPUBLICAN LAWMAKERS BREAK WITH TRUMP ON DIESEL DEAL WITH RUSSIA

Ranking defense subcommittee member Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., (L) and committee chairwoman Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, (R) look on as subcommittee chairman Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., speaks during a hearing with the Senate Appropriations Committee in the Dirksen Senate Office Building on June 11, 2025 in Washington, D.C. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

"We also recognize the urgent need to lower energy costs for American families and address the disruptions caused by the war with Iran. However, allowing Russian-origin diesel into global markets will offer limited to no relief to Americans. It will have a negligible impact on fuel prices, but the revenues the Kremlin will receive from this agreement will undoubtedly finance its desired war of attrition and advance its security cooperation with China, Iran, and North Korea. It will also endanger servicemembers operating overseas in support of Operation Epic Fury," the senators declared in their message.

"Putin is a tyrant. Withdraw from this agreement, rescind General License No. 135, and execute the authorities provided under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. Maintain our legacy – and the duty America holds – as leader of the free world," they urged.

TRUMP RUSSIA DEAL COULD FUEL PUTIN'S WAR, EX-NATO COMMANDER WARNS AS ZELENSKYY SAYS 'NYET'

U.S. President Donald Trump (R) greets Russian President Vladimir Putin as he arrives at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson on Aug. 15, 2025 in Anchorage, Alaska. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

The White House did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's comment request on Wednesday.

The senators' message to the president comes after Trump, in a Truth Social post on Friday, announced, "I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter. Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel.

TRUMP SAYS RUSSIA HAS AGREED TO DELIVER MILLIONS IN DIESEL FUEL AFTER 'HIGHLY SUCCESSFUL DISCUSSION'

"Between our TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority. This is a very big and important announcement. Additionally, it must be understood, that Iran will not have a Nuclear Weapon!" the president declared in the post.

Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: First Thing: Pope Leo recovering from surgery after lung cancer diagnosis
articles.excerpt:
Vatican says operation on US-born head of Roman Catholic church was ‘successful’. Plus, after six decades in the US, Joni Mitchell has become a citizen

Good morning. Pope Leo XIV, the head of the 1.4...
articles.body_text:
Vatican says operation on US-born head of Roman Catholic church was ‘successful’. Plus, after six decades in the US, Joni Mitchell has become a citizen

Good morning. Pope Leo XIV, the head of the 1.4 billion-strong Roman Catholic church, has been diagnosed with lung cancer. The Vatican made the announcement after Leo, 71, the first US-born leader to assume the role, underwent an operation and had the lower lobe of his right lung removed. A statement said the surgery was “successful, on schedule and as planned”.

The Vatican said Leo had “now returned to his room” after the operation. All of his appointments have been cancelled until 20 October. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, a practising Catholic who has met the pope, said he and his wife were “united in prayers” for Leo after the diagnosis.

Donald Trump faced another setback in his battle over media coverage after a federal judge ordered that journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico must still have access to the White House as the media coalition’s lawsuit against the administration plays out.

In his ruling on Tuesday, Judge Kelly wrote that the plaintiffs “are likely to succeed not only on their due process claim, but also on their two first amendment claims”. While access to the White House is not guaranteed, court precedent dictates that once it is provided to journalists, it cannot be taken away for editorial or viewpoint-based reasons.

What is the latest in Trump’s legal battle with the BBC? The BBC is asking a federal judge in Florida to force Donald Trump to sit for a deposition as part of the president’s $10bn defamation lawsuit against the British broadcaster. The president has so far declined to set a date to appear. “Plaintiff chose to file this lawsuit and, in doing so, he accepted the obligations of civil litigation,” the BBC’s motion reads. “The BBC therefore asks the court to compel plaintiff to confirm a date.”

Kimberly Guilfoyle is stepping down as US ambassador to Greece after weeks of reports that she sought payment from a Donald Trump donor in exchange for access to administration officials. The decision ends the diplomatic career of one of the US president’s longest-standing political allies.

The former fiancee of Donald Trump Jr, Guilfoyle confirmed her departure from the post which she described as the “honor of a lifetime”. She said she would “vigorously defend my name, my reputation and my integrity” and that “my commitment to President Trump, the America First movement, and the country I love will never end”.

What were the allegations against Guilfoyle? The Wall Street Journal reported she used Signal messages to press the donor Eric Deters to pay a $100,000 credit card bill in exchange for official influence – a request Deters described as a quid pro quo. She was also accused of accepting improper gifts and promoting a private Greek firm during official business. Guilfoyle strongly contests all allegations and disputes the authenticity of the messages.

Cornell University has announced it is suspending parties and other social gatherings at fraternity houses for the rest of the academic year amid intensifying backlash over its handling of allegations that a female student was sexually assaulted at a fraternity house in 2024. The university has also said it will involve New York state police in investigating alleged sex crimes on campus.

Duane “Keffe D” Davis, the former California gang leader convicted of murder for orchestrating the 1996 fatal shooting of the rapper Tupac Shakur, has been sentenced to 40 years to life in prison. Judge Carli Kierny said as she delivered the sentence: “You don’t get to take a man from his family. You don’t get to take his very life, his whole future from him and just walk away from it.” On 7 September 1996, Shakur was gunned down near the Las Vegas strip shortly after a Mike Tyson boxing match. He succumbed to his injuries days later.

Six deaths have been confirmed in Florida in the aftermath of Hurricane Isaias. The state’s governor praised Floridians and local officials for taking proper precautions, linking it to there being a lower death toll compared with previous storms.

A sixth death has been announced in Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak, as new figures show cases in the state have risen above 1,100.

An Iranian woman has been handed a death sentence for “blasphemy” in a social media post, as rights groups warn of Tehran’s increasing use of executions to suppress dissent, with at least 600 this year.

Apple has unveiled new smart home devices that showcase an upgraded Siri AI. HomeView, an iPad-like device, acts as a hub for other smart home gadgets.

Lena Dunham’s Girls is returning for a limited run at HBO. The creator and star will return along with other key cast members for a five-episode revival.

Musk’s midterm donations, mostly for rightwing candidates and causes, surpass his contributions to Trump in 2024. Meanwhile, Ukrainian soldiers in combat have suddenly had their access to Starlink satellite internet terminals restricted. Managed by Musk’s SpaceX, the terminals are a key component of Ukraine’s military operations, and the sudden restrictions led to the failure of several combat missions.

Experts say that if you’re eating any berry – strawberries, blackberries, currants, raspberries, blueberries – you’re benefiting. “All berries are good. We should eat a heck of a lot more than we do,” says Mary Ann Lila, a professor in the department of food, bioprocessing, and nutrition sciences at North Carolina State University.

My colleague Vivian Ho has been looking to find out how realistic the promises of “passive income” schemes are, and whether she could actually make money from any of them. It’s a great read.

Off the coast of Monterey, California, a team of researchers is working to restore the sunflower sea star, as 95% of these key underwater ecosystems along the Pacific coast have been decimated in past decade.

Joni Mitchell has become a US citizen, after first moving to the country in the mid-1960s. The Canada-born singer-songwriter, 82, posted footage of her citizenship ceremony on her Instagram account, saying it was “a journey that began 62 years ago”.

articles.title: Nvidia, worth $5.5tn, donates $250m to UK for AI safety research
articles.excerpt:
Pledge spanning five years from world’s most valuable firm comes as concerns about AI agents have risen

The $5.5tn (£4.1tn) US chipmaker Nvidia is donating $250m worth of computing power to the UK to...
articles.body_text:
Pledge spanning five years from world’s most valuable firm comes as concerns about AI agents have risen

The $5.5tn (£4.1tn) US chipmaker Nvidia is donating $250m worth of computing power to the UK to support AI safety research.

The donation from the world’s most valuable company comes as the UK government confirmed its AI Security Institute, which tests advance AI models, will be able to examine cutting-edge technology developed by companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google before they are released.

Nvidia said the donation, which spans five years, would “support agentic safety and security research across the UK”.

Safety concerns about AI agents – highly capable computer programs that are able to design and perform sequences of tasks autonomously – have risen since the summer, when OpenAI confirmed that a “swarm” of agents had attacked Hugging Face, a tech startup.

Nvidia did not reference AISI in its statement but said most of the money would “support the wider UK AI safety and security research community”, with a proportion of the cash going to the -led British Open-Ended Learning and Discovery Lab, the Science of Fundamental AI Research Lab – run by the Edinburgh, Cambridge, Oxford and University College London universities – and Imperial College London.

“The UK brings world-class scientific rigour to this essential engineering challenge,” said Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive. “With this $250m commitment, Nvidia will put accelerated computing in the hands of UK researchers to develop, test and strengthen safeguards for increasingly powerful AI.”

Kanishka Narayan, the UK’s AI minister, said the announcement was a “vote of confidence in our world-leading strength and expertise in AI research”.

articles.title: Israeli air strike kills Palestinian woman in Gaza City
articles.excerpt:
An Israeli air strike on an apartment block in Gaza has killed a woman and wounded two other people, hospital officials said.

Reem Asaad Awad, 33, was killed in the attack early on Wednesday in the A...
articles.body_text:
An Israeli air strike on an apartment block in Gaza has killed a woman and wounded two other people, hospital officials said.

Reem Asaad Awad, 33, was killed in the attack early on Wednesday in the Al-Rimal neighbourhood of Gaza City, the Turkish state news agency Anadolu reported, quoting a source at Al Shifa hospital.

The source said the strike caused extensive destruction to the targeted apartment and nearby buildings.

The daughter of the woman who was killed was rescued from a large fire that broke out after the attack.

Israel says it is investigating the strike and claims it targeted a member of Hamas, without providing evidence.

Reporting from Gaza City, Al Jazeera’s Ibrahim al-Khalili said the strike happened at 4am (01:00 GMT).

Israel has killed 1,501 Palestinians in Gaza since it agreed a “ceasefire” with the Palestinian group Hamas last October. The truce was part of a wider United States-backed proposal to end Israel’s genocidal war against Palestinians in Gaza.

Talks aimed at advancing to the second phase of the US plan, which includes the withdrawal of Israeli forces and the disarmament of Hamas, have stalled.

The agreement states that 600 trucks of humanitarian aid are to be allowed into Gaza each day, but Israeli authorities have continued to impose severe restrictions on supplies entering the enclave, and reconstruction of the war-shattered territory has not begun.

articles.title: Turkish police raid opposition TV station, halting live broadcasts
articles.excerpt:
Police in riot gear were seen outside the office in Istanbul early on Wednesday

Turkish police have raided the headquarters of one of the country's most-watched news channel, halting its live broadca...
articles.body_text:
Police in riot gear were seen outside the office in Istanbul early on Wednesday

Turkish police have raided the headquarters of one of the country's most-watched news channel, halting its live broadcasts.

Halk TV, which is pro-opposition, said its employees were unable to enter the building in Istanbul on Wednesday morning. The government also appointed a new administrator to run the channel.

Reports in Turkish media said financial crimes police were searching the building and 11 people had been taken into custody in the raid linked to the channel's owner.

It is the latest in a series of crackdowns on news sources deemed to be critical of Turkish President Tayyip Erdoğan and his government.

Two weeks ago, officials closed a leading news site because of what they called its "LGBT propaganda".

Halk's news channel and live broadcasts on its YouTube page were both offline early on Wednesday.

The channel has been seen by many in the country as being close to the opposition Republican People's Party (CHP). It often voices criticism of Erdoğan's ruling AK party.

Prosecutors said arrest warrants had been issued for 17 people as part of the investigation into Halk chairman Cafer Mahiroğlu on allegations of bribery, rigging tenders and money laundering, Turkish media reported.

Mahiroğlu, who was reportedly not in the country during the raid, wrote on social media that seven members of his family were among those detained.

"Today is a dark day for Turkey," he said in a video message. "The public's right to information is being seized for political reasons."

The Istanbul Bar Association denounced the move, which it noted came hours before Ekrem Imamoğlu, widely seen as Erdoğan's biggest political rival, was due to begin his defence against corruption charges in court, for which he has been in prison for over a year.

A Halk TV staff member shared images of police stood beside a TV studio during the raid

Özgür Özel, leader of the opposition New Party, called the raid "weak and cowardly".

"Storming a TV channel with a police raid at dawn and appointing a trustee is something only dictators do," he wrote on social media.

Özel set up the party after being removed as the CHP's leader by a court in May and replaced by a party veteran who had previously been voted out, in a move which further cemented Erdoğan's grip on power.

Turkey ranked 163rd out of 180 countries in the Reporters Without Borders (RSF) 2026 World Press Freedom Index, external.

The organisation stated that 90% of national media outlets were under government control and criticised the "abusive prosecution" of critical publications in the country, which Erdoğan has led since 2003.

The vast majority of Turkish media is seen as pro-government after years of state legal and financial pressure, corporate acquisitions and self-censorship.

In September, a court ordered the blocking of access to the website and social media accounts of T24, on the grounds that it had published "LGBT propaganda".

In October 2025, the authorities seized control of Tele1, another pro-opposition TV channel, appointing a trustee to oversee broadcasts, which were stripped of all hard-news content.

The channel still exists but its pro-opposition stance has been completely neutralised.

Turkey demands more than 2,000 years in jail for popular Istanbul mayor

articles.title: Ukrainian soldiers in combat have access to Starlink satellite internet restricted
articles.excerpt:
Outage of terminals managed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX comes as Russia launches ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from US

Ukrainian soldiers in combat have suddenly had their acces...
articles.body_text:
Outage of terminals managed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX comes as Russia launches ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from US

Ukrainian soldiers in combat have suddenly had their access to Starlink satellite internet terminals restricted as the Trump administration has increased pressure on Ukraine to halt long-range strikes on Russia’s oil industry immediately.

The terminals, which are distributed and managed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, are a key component of Ukraine’s military operations and the sudden restrictions on the terminals travelling at high speeds on Tuesday evening led to the failure of several combat missions, said an adviser on military technology to Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

The sudden outage came as Russia launched ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US for a second night. For years, the US has provided Ukraine with intelligence when strikes were about to take place.

Donald Trump has denied that his administration has cut intelligence sharing with Ukraine. Zelenskyy also indicated that the US was continuing to share intelligence with Ukraine in an interview with NPR aired on Wednesday, but confirmed that military advisers had received threats from the US that intelligence sharing could be limited.

Ukraine did not receive any warning before Russia launched its first barrage of ballistic missiles on Tuesday evening, according to Col Yurii Ihnat, a spokesperson for the air force. But it did receive warnings from “foreign partners” about three subsequent barrages, leaving further confusion about whether or not the US is intentionally withholding intelligence from Ukraine.

SpaceX did not confirm any changes to Starlink’s functionality and it was not immediately clear why the restrictions had been put in place. Terminals travelling at more than 100mph and using a version of Starlink for the military and other national security agencies suddenly lost connectivity, said Serhiy Beskrestnov, in what appeared to be a targeted outage meant to disrupt military operations.

“Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” said Beskrestnov, who is also a popular military blogger. “It’s clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation.”

Limiting Starlink’s access speeds would have a significant effect on Ukraine’s mid-range strike campaign, where it uses the satellite internet system to navigate drones to hit targets behind the front in Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine. But there have been no reports that access for static Starlink terminals have been cut, meaning critical battlefield communications for soldiers should remain unaffected. The detection of incoming Russian missiles and drones relies on other technologies.

Musk, an ally of Trump, had previously cut off Starlink service to Ukrainian soldiers during an offensive that took a small amount of Russian territory.

Serhii Sternenko, a political activist with close ties to the military, first reported the outage and later said that the speeds at which the loss of connectivity occurred had fallen even lower. “It is likely that the company ‘SpaceX’ resorted to such measures at the request of the Trump administration,” he said. “Ordinary satellite communication terminals are currently operational.”

Trump has demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian oil refineries, which he has blamed for the high cost of diesel, although most analysts say that the closure of the strait of Hormuz has had a far larger impact on global energy prices.

Zelenskyy had suggested, though not said, that the US was intentionally withholding intelligence from Ukraine about impending Russian missile strikes.

Russia carried out a massive strike against Ukrainian energy infrastructure late on Tuesday evening, Zelenskyy said, launching 39 ballistic missiles and 120 attack drones against Kyiv and Kharkiv. The strikes hit several power plants and key substations that carry electricity to the capital, including from a major power plant.

“The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States,” he said. “Russia does not consider the American president’s statements strong.”

At least 600,000 people were now without power, he said, adding that outages could become even more widespread.

articles.title: Russian strikes leave 600,000 without power in Ukraine, as Starlink restrictions affect front line
articles.excerpt:
Watch: What we know about Russia's overnight strikes on Ukraine

At least 600,000 people in Ukraine are without electricity after deadly overnight Russian missile and drone strikes, President Volodymy...
articles.body_text:
Watch: What we know about Russia's overnight strikes on Ukraine

At least 600,000 people in Ukraine are without electricity after deadly overnight Russian missile and drone strikes, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.

He said "critical" energy infrastructure had been hit in Kyiv and the capital region, and in the north-eastern city of Kharkiv – despite US President Donald Trump's claim on Sunday that an "energy ceasefire" was in place between Russia and Ukraine.

Three people were killed in Kyiv, officials said. Russia said its "massive" strikes had hit communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military.

Separately, Zelensky's adviser said speed restrictions on the Starlink communications network had disrupted Ukrainian battlefield "missions".

In Wednesday's post on Telegram, Serhiy Beskrestnov said Elon Musk's SpaceX company had "implemented overnight a speed limit on Starlink terminals".

He said Ukrainian troops had not been informed about this, and the speed limits – set at 100mph (160km/h) – had already resulted in "the disruption of a number of missions".

"It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation," Beskrestnov said.

In the follow-up post, he stressed that Starlink was the most effective tool for enabling interceptors to shoot down Russia's newly developed jet-propelled drones.

The Starlink system has become a vital tool to give troops in Ukraine internet access

A source in the Ukrainian defence ministry later told the BBC: "Last night, we detected restrictions affecting Starlink connectivity at speeds above 160 km/h, although we are still verifying the exact speed threshold.

"This situation is significantly complicating operations, particularly logistics, unmanned systems, middle-strike missions, and other activities," the source said, adding the "root cause" of the issue was being investigated.

The Starlink system has become a vital tool to give troops in Ukraine internet access, allowing them to effectively control drones heading towards Russian targets.

In February, Musk's decision to deny Russian forces access to Starlink blunted Moscow's advance in Ukraine and caused confusion among Russian commanders.

Musk's SpaceX has not commented on the reported speed restrictions.

Zelensky has said the US threatened to restrict intelligence sharing if he did not sign up to Trump's energy ceasefire. Trump on Tuesday denied that Washington was withholding intelligence.

Ukraine's air force said that overnight, Russia had launched 39 ballistic and cruise missiles and 128 drones, and that four of those missiles and 115 drones had been shot down.

It is the second night in a row Kyiv has been hit by Russian missiles, and comes as Zelensky prepares to meet UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham at Downing Street on Wednesday to discuss accelerating air defence supplies to Kyiv.

During the past two nights, ballistic missiles have struck targets in the Ukrainian capital without any warning, before air raid sirens could be sounded.

Ukraine relies on US satellite systems to track Russian missiles in order to issue alerts and to try to shoot them down.

People watched the emergency services at work at the scene of the strikes in Ukraine

Meanwhile, the Russian defence ministry said 902 Ukrainian drones had been shot down overnight over a number of Russian regions, including the capital Moscow and Crimea – Ukraine's southern peninsula annexed by Russia in 2014.

On Sunday, Trump wrote in a post on social media: "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!"

Zelensky has since repeatedly said Ukraine is ready to halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries and other energy facilities if Moscow did the same.

But Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring. Under any truce, he added, Europe would be able to "pump [Ukraine] with new weapons", enabling it to continue the war.

Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

Russia's offensive ability is broken, Kyiv's former top general tells BBC

Six Ukrainian energy sites hit by Russia since Trump announced ceasefire, Zelensky says

articles.title: Russian attacks on Ukraine leave 600,000 without power as Zelenskyy says Moscow ‘disrespecting’ US – Europe live
articles.excerpt:
Zelenskyy says Russia attacked ‘infrastructure covered by the ceasefire announced by the American president’

Ukrainian soldiers have access to Starlink satellite internet restricted

“Russia has neve...
articles.body_text:
Zelenskyy says Russia attacked ‘infrastructure covered by the ceasefire announced by the American president’

Ukrainian soldiers have access to Starlink satellite internet restricted

“Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States,” Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, after a night of relentless attacks on Ukraine’s infrastructure, despite Donald Trump’s claims of an energy ceasefire.

“A targeted Russian ballistic missile strike specifically against energy infrastructure – the very infrastructure covered by the ceasefire announced by the American President. The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale,” he said.

At least 600,000 people were left without power this morning, with temperatures falling below 10 degrees Celsius in Kyiv.

Meanwhile, a senior aide to Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine has been left struggling after Starlink satellite connection speeds were apparently restricted, complicating military operations on the ground.

Serhii Beskrestnov, widely known by his call sign, Flash, said:

“Our defence forces received no warning about this restriction, and it led to the disruption of a number of missions. Clearly, this action cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation.”

Ukraine’s Zelenskyy is expected in London today for talks with the UK’s prime minister, Andy Burnham, so we will probably hear more from him.

Elsewhere, Nato’s secretary general Mark Rutte will visit Estonia this morning, and Germany’s embattled chancellor Friedrich Merz is scheduled to address the Bundestag with a statement on the EU and Ukraine this afternoon.

And Pope Leo had a “peaceful night” at Rome’s Gemelli hospital after yesterday’s surgery which confirmed lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer.

I will bring you all the updates throughout the day.

It’s Wednesday, 14 October 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

The European Commission has warned that the EU is “headed for a very, very difficult winter” with high energy prices expected to cause an affordability crisis and “a very volatile” in the energy markets.

The warning was delivered by the EU’s energy spokesperson Anna-Kaisa Itkonen when answering questions about proposed changes adding flexibility to rules on methane imports to help save costs.

She stressed the EU was “not facing a security supply issue for the time being,” but it faced a “very unpredictable” situation in the coming months.

“We do not have visibility, for example, what and when something will happen in the Strait of Hormuz, where 20% of gas and oil is being blocked since many, many months,” she said.

The commission’s chief spokesperson, Paula Pinho, added that the changes are needed as “we could not anticipate that we would have a crisis in the Strait of Hormuz,” which continues to affect prices and supply of energy.

This summer in Germany, Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) booked a historic state election victory in Saxony-Anhalt. Meanwhile, support for far-right parties has been growing across Europe.

There are now radical right, populist parties in coalition governments in Croatia, Czechia, Italy and Finland, and leading in the polls in Austria, Belgium, France and Germany.

The coming months will see further crucial elections, beginning in Spain in November and continuing in France, Estonia, Finland, Greece, Slovakia, Poland and Italy next year. How might these elections shape the political future of the continent?

Jon Henley and Ashifa Kassam, our European correspondents, will be answering your questions live on Reddit r/geopolitics from 4pm CEST.

Rutte gets asked “is Russia foolish enough to consider attacking any of Nato countries?”

He says “we don’t think so” and that there is “no imminent threat against Nato territory,” but stresses that “if we see a build up, we will react to it.”

He says Nato’s message – as also expressed by the alliance’s top commander, Alexus Grynkewich earlier this week – is clear: “we will defend every inch of our territory, whether people live there or not.”

“We will never, ever mount a attack towards anyone else because that is not in our interest. We are a defensive alliance.”

And that concludes their press conference.

In the Q&A, Rutte gets asked about the growing speculations that the US intelligence sharing with Ukraine may have stopped, after Zelenskyy’s repeated complains that Kyiv had no notice of recent attacks.

He says Trump “was very clear yesterday … that intelligence sharing has not stopped.”

More broadly on Russia, he says Nato has “all the response options we need,” although “you will not always see them; they will not always be public.”

“But here’s the main thing: we are stronger. Russia is not in a good place. These hybrid attacks, whatever it is, are a sign of weakness. What they allow us to do is to talk about it the whole day and to be rattled and to have press conferences on it. We’re not going to do that. We will react where we need to react.”

Nato’s Rutte thanks Estonia for the role it plays in Nato, before turning to Ukraine.

He says “with winter coming and with Russia’s aggression unrelenting, allies need to do more, especially in support of air defence.”

He says “Russia continues its attacks on Ukrainian civilians and it continues its hybrid campaign against NATO allies.”

“Putin is trying to weaken our resolve and stop our support for Ukraine, but Russia is failing. It is failing on the battlefield in Ukraine and we will not be intimidated.”

Nato’s secretary general Mark Rutte is now appearing at a press conference with Estonia’s prime minister Kristen Michal.

Michal says that “supporting Ukraine is part of our own security,” as he warns that “Russia’s goals have not changed” and Moscow is “testing our unity with hybrid attacks and tries to divert our attention from Ukraine to elsewhere.”

“Russia wants us to focus on our problems and get tired of supporting Ukraine. We should not let it happen. Estonia will continue to support Ukraine militarily this year.”

He says “our task is to help Ukraine resist Russia’s brutal attacks,” and help it with more weapons and air defence.

“We are learning from Ukraine every day. Ukrainian experience is invaluable for developing our defence capability and defence industry … Ukraine’s NATO membership would, in the long run be the strongest security guarantee.”

Michal says “Russia must know that Nato is ready” as it defends allies and supports Ukraine.

Ukrainian soldiers in combat have suddenly had their access to Starlink satellite internet terminals restricted (9:57, 10:16) as the Trump administration has increased pressure on Ukraine to halt long-range strikes on Russia’s oil industry immediately.

The terminals, which are distributed and managed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, are a key component of Ukraine’s military operations and the sudden restrictions on the high-speed terminals on Tuesday evening led to the failure of several combat missions, said an adviser on military technology to Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

The sudden outage came as Russia launched ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US for a second night. For years the US has provided Ukraine with intelligence when strikes were about to take place.

Terminals travelling at more than 100mph and using a version of Starlink for the military and other national security agencies suddenly lost connectivity, said Serhiy Beskrestnov, in what appeared to be a targeted outage meant to disrupt military operations.

“Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” said Beskrestnov, who is also a popular military blogger. “It’s clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation.”

A Ukrainian soldier is to go on trial in Hamburg accused of taking part in one of the most brazen acts of sabotage in postwar European history – the 2022 attack on the Nord Stream gas pipelines between Russia and Germany.

Serhii Kuznetsov, a special forces officer from the Ukrainian military, is accused by prosecutors of being an accomplice to war crimes by attacking civilian infrastructure, causing an explosion, damaging property and disrupting public services.

Kuznetsov, who will be identified in the trial opening on Wednesday just as Serhii K due to German privacy laws, was referenced by his full name in an extradition order. He is alleged to have prepared and carried out the detonation of at least four incendiary devices of up to 27kg in weight at a depth of about 80 metres under the Baltic Sea, close to the Danish island of Bornholm.

He is believed to have had six accomplices, including four deep-sea divers, an explosives expert and a ship’s captain, who are alleged to have used a rented yacht and timer-controlled explosives. Both he and his country deny any involvement in the attacks.

The explosions took place on 26 September 2022, badly damaging the pipelines which had been constructed to carry Russian natural gas between Vyborg in western Russia and Lubmin, near Greifswald in northern Germany.

The blasts caused the Nord Stream 1 pipelines – Russia’s main gas supply route to Germany before Moscow cut the supplies in August 2022 – to burst. They also damaged Nord Stream 2, which was ready to carry gas but was never put into operation after Germany suspended its authorisation process just before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The attacks happened as European countries were seeking to transition away from Russian energy supplies in reaction to the Kremlin’s aggression.

They exposed the dependence of Europe – and, in particular, Germany – on Russian gas as well as highlighting the murkiness of underground operations during wartime.

Security observers initially blamed Moscow for the attack. Russia has denied involvement, in turn blaming the US, which has denied it just as forcefully.

However, in July German state prosecutors accused Ukrainian “state authorities” of ordering the attack, arguing: “The aim was to permanently halt gas supplies via the pipelines and prevent Russia from using the revenue from natural gas trade to finance its war effort.”

The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has denied his country was involved.

Sixteen trial dates have been scheduled at Hamburg’s Hanseatic higher regional court up to and including 17 December, with further hearings likely in January and February.

Poland’s foreign minister Radosław Sikorski has taken to X to confront the platform’s billionaire owner Elon Musk over reported restrictions to Starlink in Ukraine.

Poland helps Ukraine to foot the bill for Starlink, which provides crucial internet connectivity to Kyiv and its military, and says it pays some $50m a year.

“Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again? As your European customers, we are watching you.”

The pair repeatedly clashed in the past, with annoyed Musk telling Sikorski last year to be “quiet.”

Meanwhile, Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni said the US deal with Russia over diesel supply is “a very risky choice,” with “clear” risks.

“The outcome ​of this decision is ‌uncertain, while the ‌risks are clear,” Meloni told the Italian parliament.

“It provides Moscow with legitimacy as its bombs continue to fall on Ukrainian cities, generates new revenue to finance the war, and implicitly weakens the effectiveness of sanctions,” she added.

The Italian PM also returned to the idea that the EU27 should appoint “an authoritative figure” to lead talks with Russia and Ukraine.

The overnight attacks killed at least three people in Kyiv, authorities said.

Mayor Vitaly Klitschko reported overnight that “a massive ballistic missile strike” against the capital hit its energy facilities, causing power outages across the city.

Wednesday’s Russian attacks also targeted state railway facilities in five regions across Ukraine, said prime ⁠minister Sergii Koretskyi.
