articles.title: Mamdani, City Council move to end iconic NYC horse-drawn carriage industry as workers face uncertain future
articles.excerpt:
Deepak Mahajan listens as his video statement is played for the New York City Council, saying their son would still be alive if lawmakers had passed a horse-drawn carriage ban last year. (WNYW)

New Y...
articles.body_text:
Deepak Mahajan listens as his video statement is played for the New York City Council, saying their son would still be alive if lawmakers had passed a horse-drawn carriage ban last year. (WNYW)

New York City's iconic horse-drawn carriages could disappear from Central Park under an agreement reached Tuesday between Mayor Zohran Mamdani and City Council Speaker Julie Menin, setting the stage for a vote to eliminate the historic industry.

The agreement would ban horse-drawn carriage operations beginning June 1, 2028, if approved by the City Council on Oct. 22, ending a longtime tourist attraction amid concerns over animal welfare and public safety.

The proposed legislation, known as Romanch's Law — named after 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan, who suffered fatal injuries in a horse-drawn carriage crash in June — would require city officials to develop a transition plan for carriage drivers, owners and stable workers, though financial compensation would not be guaranteed.

MAMDANI'S LATEST FREEBIE SETS OFF ONLINE FURY AS CRITICS RIP CITY PRIORITIES: 'OPERA SOCIALISM'

A horse-drawn carriage travels through Central Park in New York City in 2024. An 18-year-old passenger was killed in June after a carriage reportedly bolted and overturned in the park. (Luiz C. Ribeiro/New York Daily News/Tribune News Service via Getty Images, File)

"The horse carriage industry is coming to an end in New York City. Our administration will make sure workers and owners are protected, and the horses are safe," Mamdani wrote on X.

Animal rights group PETA celebrated the agreement after years of campaigning against the carriage industry.

"This is long overdue, and it can't come quickly enough," PETA representative Ashley Byrne told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview Tuesday.

Byrne cited incidents involving horses collapsing in city streets and colliding with vehicles, and said more than 70% of New Yorkers support a ban, a figure Fox News Digital has not independently verified.

MAMDANI, NYPD GIVE SECURITY UPDATE AHEAD OF JEWISH HIGH HOLY DAYS, 9/11 25TH ANNIVERSARY

Emergency responders gather around an overturned horse-drawn carriage in Central Park after 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan was fatally injured when the carriage reportedly collided with another carriage and flipped over in June. (WNYW)

The Central Park Conservancy also welcomed the agreement, emphasizing public safety.

"We applaud the City Council for finally taking on this issue. For the Central Park Conservancy, this has always been a matter of public safety. We hope carriages can be phased out efficiently and humanely so that no one else ever suffers the fate of Romanch Mahajan," Conservancy President and CEO Betsy Smith said.

But the Transport Workers Union sharply criticized the agreement, accusing city leaders of failing to provide meaningful financial protections for workers and carriage owners.

"Council Speaker Menin's bill has no meaningful economic relief for workers," TWU International President John Samuelsen said in a statement. "It only says the city should prepare a worker transition plan by April 2027 and include weak measures like job fairs and job counseling."

Samuelsen also accused Menin of exploiting the June death of 18-year-old tourist Romanch Mahajan to advance the ban.

MAMDANI'S 'THIS IS ONLY THE BEGINNING' ANNOUNCEMENT CRACKING DOWN ON FOOD DELIVERY TIPS SPARKS OUTRAGE

Julie Menin, speaker of the New York City Council. (John Lamparski/Bloomberg via Getty Images, File)

"Council Speaker Menin used the tragic death of a tourist to contrive a public safety crisis. This is disgraceful political opportunism, and Zohran should not simply go along with it, particularly when immigrant families' livelihoods are being destroyed," he said.

Under the legislation, city agencies would have until April 1, 2027, to develop a workforce transition plan that includes job placement, career counseling, training and referrals to other transportation and tourism jobs. Officials would also have to consider compensation for carriage owners and assistance with retiring horses, but no payouts are guaranteed.

"We have been working closely with the City Council, union partners, carriage drivers, animal welfare advocates, and community leaders to deliver a just transition that protects workers while ending horse-drawn carriages in Central Park once and for all," City Hall spokesperson Sneha Choudhary said.

Tow truck workers load an overturned horse-drawn carriage from the fatal accident near Tavern on the Green, June 17, in Manhattan, N.Y. (TNS)

Fox News Digital reached out to Transport Workers Union Local 100, which represents carriage drivers and owners, for comment.

Menin, who would be the first sitting City Council speaker to support the legislation, according to the Council, said the city must balance tradition with public safety and workers' livelihoods.

"We can honor our city's traditions while recognizing when it's time to move forward in the interest of public safety, protecting workers, and strengthening our city's economic vitality," Menin said.

The legislation follows the June death Mahajan, a tourist from India who suffered fatal injuries after a horse-drawn carriage bolted, collided with another carriage and overturned in Central Park.

"The tragic and preventable death of 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan made clear that the status quo is no longer acceptable," Menin said.

The Central Park Conservancy previously reported that the fatal crash was the eighth horse-related incident in or around the park in approximately 13 months. Days earlier, a carriage horse named Deniz reportedly collapsed and died while pulling tourists.

Following Mahajan's death, TWU Local 100 called for tougher driver examinations, enhanced training and additional safety regulations rather than an outright ban.Mamdani's office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

articles.body_text:
Karen Holt, an associate professor of criminal justice at Michigan State University, discussed fears of a possible serial killer in Lansing, Michigan, and warned residents to avoid the Lansing River Trail following five deaths.

Concerns over a possible serial killer in Lansing, Michigan, have the Big Ten college town on edge.

Earlier this month, the Lansing Police Department announced it is investigating the unnerving possibility that five recent deaths may be connected to an attacker allegedly lurking along the Lansing River Trail.

"I definitely think we need to be cautious, but we also need to be rational," Karen Holt, a criminology professor at Michigan State University, told Fox News Digital.

The Lansing River Trail near to where Louis Woodruff was critically injured and later died in the 300 block of East Oakland Avenue on Wednesday, Sept. 16, 2026, in Lansing. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

MAN PLEADS GUILTY TO 2023 KILLING OF LAUREN HEIKE ON PHOENIX HIKING TRAIL

Police said over the last year five men were attacked along the popular trail; one of the victims was found stabbed to death under a bridge.

"As someone who studies violence, the first thing that came to mind was the victims and the vulnerability of these victims and the method of the violence," Holt said.

HUD’S HOMELESSNESS REFORMS PUT HUMAN LIVES AHEAD OF HOUSING BUREAUCRACY

The Lansing River Trail near the 200 block of East Cesar Chavez Avenue on Wednesday, Sept. 16, 2026, in Lansing. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

All the victims were homeless, police said.

CRIMINAL PROFILER REVEALS 'EXTREMELY RARE' RED FLAG IN CASE OF SUSPECTED SERIAL KILLER MIGRANT IN TEXAS

"If we have a community where people can be attacked in this way, then I don't necessarily know that we can call it a safe community," Holt said.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Lansing Police Chief Rob Backus speaks about the string of recent deaths along the Lansing River Trail during a press conference on Friday, Oct. 2, 2026, at police headquarters in downtown Lansing. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

She continued, saying, "One of the patterns with either single or serial homicide offenders or just violent offenders is that they tend to go after individuals who are particularly vulnerable."

She says homicide offenders often see these victims as individuals "who lack credibility" and may assume that going after homeless victims "decreases the likelihood that they're going to be caught."

‘OUT OF CONTROL’ KILLINGS IN SPANBERGER’S VIRGINIA REACH ‘INSANE’ POINT AS MIGRANT CHARGED IN STABBING SPREE

Police in Lansing, Michigan, are investigating a possible serial killer who may be linked to five deaths along the Lansing River Trail. (FOX2 Detroit)

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

On September 3, Edward Joseph Smith, 23, was arrested in connection to the deadly stabbing of Daniel Lusk, 22.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB

"I would love to learn more about the relationship between that victim and perpetrator," she said. Police have not announced any motive in Lusk's murder.

PHILADELPHIA HOME LINKED TO 7 MISSING WOMEN, LATE RESIDENT'S POTENTIAL 'SERIAL KILLER' MEMOIR INVESTIGATED

Smith has not been accused of any crime or wrongdoing in the four other deaths.

Lansing Police are investigating a possible serial killer. (USA Today Network via Reuters Connect)

Holt says Lusk's murder "stands out" in comparison to the other alleged killings in that the victim was stabbed – whereas the other four victims suffered some sort of head injury or possible blunt force trauma.

TOLEDO POLICE FOLLOWING 'MULTIPLE LEADS' AS MANHUNT ENTERS 3RD DAY AFTER FESTIVAL SHOOTING

Police have yet to confirm any arrest of this possible serial killer.

Holt maintains Lansing needs to remain vigilant.

"Don't walk the trail would be my advice. Maybe walk a different trail."

articles.title: Trump administration slashes time refugees have to challenge loss of legal status
articles.excerpt: Federal immigration rule lawsuits from blue cities spark reaction from former Acting DHS Secretary Chad Wolf. Sanctuary cities, including New York City, prepare legal action as a Department of Homelan...
articles.body_text:
Federal immigration rule lawsuits from blue cities spark reaction from former Acting DHS Secretary Chad Wolf. Sanctuary cities, including New York City, prepare legal action as a Department of Homeland Security social media post suggests sanctuary states are terrified they will lose vital federal funds under the new policy guidelines implemented by the administration.

The Trump administration is adopting a new rule that would shorten the time refugees have to challenge the termination of their legal status, marking another restriction on legal immigration pathways as the White House continues its immigration enforcement crackdown.

The new policy, which takes effect Wednesday without undergoing the usual advance public notice-and-comment process, reduces the time refugees have to respond to a notice of intent to terminate their status from 30 days to 10.

According to the new rule, the administration is aiming to "mitigate potential risks" linked to people who were admitted as refugees but were not eligible for refugee status.

The documents pointed to refugees admitted during the Biden administration, claiming there was an "alarming erosion of the integrity" of the refugee program during those years, although refugee advocates dispute that allegation.

TRUMP ADMIN PAUSES VISA APPOINTMENTS WORLDWIDE AMID HEIGHTENED SCREENING FOR APPLICANTS

The Trump administration is adopting a new rule that would cut the time refugees have to challenge the termination of their legal status. (Photo by Jim WATSON / AFP via Getty Images)

"A review of refugee processing policies and procedures implemented under the Biden administration indicates an alarming erosion of integrity leading to aliens being admitted to the United States as refugees when their identities, eligibility for refugee classification, and admissibility were determined based on incomplete records," DHS' document reads.

"The priority of expediency over quality encouraged a lack of robust interviews," it added. "Certain questions to ensure that aliens were eligible for refugee status prior to admission to the United States were omitted and this increased the risk of ineligible aliens being approved for refugee classification and subsequently admitted to the United States."

A spokesman for Citizenship and Immigration Services, Zach Kahler, similarly said the agency has found "an alarming erosion of screening and vetting measures" during the Biden administration to "rush processing and maximize the number of refugees admitted."

The Trump administration is "ensuring that refugee status is reserved only for those who were eligible under the law," he said in a statement to The Associated Press.

This comes after the Trump administration ordered the review of at least 185,000 refugees admitted during the Biden administration who still have pending green card applications.

The U.S. refugee admissions program has historically enjoyed bipartisan support since Congress passed the Refugee Act of 1980. Refugees undergo extensive security screenings and background checks before being approved for resettlement. Many spend years waiting in refugee camps before they can be admitted after undergoing multiple rounds of interviews and screenings.

The Trump administration ordered the review of at least 185,000 refugees admitted during the Biden administration who still have pending green card applications. (John Moore/Getty Images)

With the Trump administration's new rule, critics argue tens of thousands of people who fled persecution and wars in their home countries could be forced into deportation.

"These families did everything asked of them," Krish O’Mara Vignarajah, president of Global Refuge, said in a statement. "They submitted to interviews, background checks and years of waiting abroad, only setting foot on U.S. soil once government officials approved their applications."

She said the Department of Homeland Security now wants to "revisit those decisions on a 10-day clock, a notice period wholly insufficient to find a lawyer, translate documents or get records out of a country they were forced to flee due to conflict or persecution."

"In some cases, refugees may not even receive the notice before their ten days are up, effectively eliminating their only chance to respond," she added. "If the government’s case for termination is truly strong, it can afford to give people a meaningful chance to challenge it."

HIAS, a major refugee aid group, also warned that refugees who have fled violence, persecution and displacement will be at risk of being deported to countries where they could be subject to persecution and torture.

"They are trying to upend the core principle that refugee resettlement represents permanent protection," HIAS Vice President Naomi Steinberg said in a statement.

FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION FINES OF UP TO $1.8M FOR MIGRANTS

The Trump administration is aiming to "mitigate potential risks" linked to people who were admitted as refugees but were not eligible for refugee status. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)

The Trump administration has significantly overhauled the U.S. refugee admissions program, sharply restricting overall admissions while prioritizing the resettlement of white South Africans.

Last month, the Trump administration established a ceiling of 17,500 refugee admissions for fiscal year 2027, with most slots allocated to Afrikaners, a predominantly white ethnic group in South Africa.

During his first term, President Donald Trump reduced the number of refugees approved every year. The Biden administration reversed that trend, setting a refugee admissions ceiling of 125,000 for fiscal year 2025.

When Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, he immediately suspended the refugee program, stranding people around the world who had been set to come to the U.S. The administration later reopened the program but limited it mostly to white South Africans.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Barriers facing black and south Asian music events ‘cost London up to £141m a year’
articles.excerpt:
Exclusive: Investigation finds racial inequality in live music industry rife and many genres labelled ‘high risk’ despite lack of evidence

Black and south Asian music events in London face disproport...
articles.body_text:
Exclusive: Investigation finds racial inequality in live music industry rife and many genres labelled ‘high risk’ despite lack of evidence

Black and south Asian music events in London face disproportionate cancellations, restrictions and licensing barriers compared with white events, according to a two-year investigation into racial inequality in the capital’s live music industry.

The Race Equality in Music Event Licensing (REMEL) report, led by Black Lives in Music, estimates that cancellations, displacement and events prevented from taking place cost London £127m to £141m annually, with projected losses exceeding £650m over five years.

The report found that genres including Afrobeats, drill and dancehall are routinely labelled “high risk” despite a lack of credible evidence, while indie, pop and rock events face comparatively little scrutiny.

Other events facing stringent restrictions included reggae gatherings aimed at older audiences, jazz nights and community events.

The research raised concerns over the use of unverified police intelligence, with promoters describing events being cancelled based on undisclosed information, online searches or unrelated incidents.

Charisse Beaumont, chief executive of Black Lives in Music, said that although the investigation focused on London, the problems it uncovered exist nationwide.

“As soon as we put the report out there, the call for our survey, people were upset that they couldn’t complete the survey because they were outside of London,” she said.

For Beaumont, the discrimination extended far beyond specific music genres. “It’s about race. And that’s what’s so deeply sad about it.”

The two-year study was commissioned by the mayor’s office and included collaboration by the Greater London Authority (GLA), the Metropolitan Police Service, UK Music, LIVE, the Musicians’ Union and a wide network of promoters, artists, venue operators and community representatives.

The findings suggest that the legacy of the Metropolitan police’s controversial Form 696 persists. Introduced in 2005 as a risk assessment tool, it was scrapped in 2017 after criticism that it discriminated against black music events.

Hakeem Stevens, the report’s lead researcher, said police scrutiny had become harder to document. “Back in the day when emails were sent and faxes were sent, we had documented evidence. Now what’s happening is it’s whispers, it’s phone calls, it’s conversations, verbal conversations that can’t be recorded.”

He said black and Asian performers faced disproportionate scrutiny, adding: “You’ve got white artists that perform black music, and they don’t get given that level of scrutiny.”

Researchers found that promoters received little explanation for cancellations, faced substantial security costs and had limited opportunities to challenge decisions.

Stevens said the financial and reputational consequences could severely affect mental health.

Beaumont highlighted the case of the Colour Factory, a black-owned venue whose licence was suspended after an incident outside its premises that was reportedly unrelated to the venue.

She said the owner successfully challenged the decision but faced significant financial losses, including legal costs and staff redundancies.

“In the end, they won, but they didn’t get their money back,” she said.

The report also found that when incidents occur, many white-owned venues are supported back into business after incidents, while black-owned venues are forced to close for prolonged periods.

Kwame Otiende, a venue owner, promoter and Green councillor, said the additional scrutiny discouraged venues from hosting certain events.

“Venues will have known that they get a lot more grief from whatever relevant authorities they need to go through to get a temporary event notice,” he said.

Instead, he suggested, venues may opt for safer commercial choices: “I could just put your very sort of middle-of-the-road chart music … and I’ll still make the same amount of money.”

The report sets out 19 recommendations, including calls for more transparent, evidence-based licensing decisions, alongside an independent review, clearer evidence standards, better reporting of licensing outcomes and stronger accountability.

Beaumont said: “Success would be for me, the ability for any artist from any background, particularly Black and south Asian, to be able to perform and put on events at any venue without barriers, so they too can make money

“They’ve got an album out, they do a tour, they might be able to do a 1,000-capacity venue, but can they progress from 2,000 to 5,000 to 20,000 to stadium? That doesn’t happen for us.”

The Met police commander Neerav Patel said the force would carefully consider the reports finding. “Our focus will remain on making fair, evidence-based contributions to the licensing process which balance the interests of venues, promoters, artists and local communities while never compromising on our ultimate priority which is to keep Londoners safe” said Patel.

Beau Lamarre-Condon previously visited a farm where he later tried to sink the bodies of Jesse Baird and Luke Davies, the prosecution has told a Sydney court.

The rural property belonged to the family of a man the police officer had met on a dating app and the two visited the farm together months before the alleged murders.

Lamarre-Condon, 31, has been accused of shooting dead Baird and Davies with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024.

He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.

The prosecution on Wednesday read out a statement from Michael Cella who was 20 years old when he spoke with police in 2024. Cella said he matched with Lamarre-Condon on the dating app Hinge in March 2023.

They began seeing each other, with the pair going to Bondi Junction to watch Hunger Games and the Taylor Swift movie in late 2023. They also ate sushi together.

In November 2023, Lamarre-Condon invited the younger man on a weekend trip to a cabin.

But because the proposed trip was too expensive, Cella invited the police officer to go to his family’s hobby farm in Bungonia.

The property had four dams, animals, a fence and a front gate with chains and a padlock, the court heard on Wednesday.

On 6 November, they drove around the area, looked at the animals and stayed overnight, with Lamarre-Condon recording the farm and posting it to his Instagram story with the Taylor Swift song You Belong With Me.

Cella later learned about Baird when he saw Lamarre-Condon’s Instagram posts with him.

“Beau told me they were friends. I sensed there was something more and Beau was not telling me everything,” Cella said in his 2024 statement read to the jury.

Communication between Lamarre-Condon and Cella slowed significantly about mid-November 2023 and the latter soon lost interest.

He received some messages from Lamarre-Condon in January 2024 but ignored them, blocked his contact number and deleted their text message conversation, the court heard.

Days later, he received a call from a number with no called ID and did not answer, followed by a message on the encrypted messaging app Signal from a contact with the name Bob. Cella did not respond.

After the deaths of Baird and Davies, Lamarre-Condon allegedly made an unsuccessful attempt to sink their bodies at the bottom of a dam at Cella Farm, the prosecution has told the jury.

They were later found at the fence line of a monastery about 20km from the property.

The defence has not disputed the officer attempted to clean up the scene or dispose of the bodies, claiming he “panicked considerably” after acting in self-defence.

But the events inside Baird’s home are contested.

The defence has argued the couple were accidentally shot in two separate struggles.

The prosecution has told the court that Lamarre-Condon shot Baird twice in the kitchen before shooting Davies through a bedroom door.

A computer-generated video outlining the crown’s version of events was played to the New South Wales supreme court jury earlier on Wednesday.

The 3D recreation of the Paddington terrace on the morning of the shootings allowed the jury to see the path Lamarre-Condon allegedly took through the home. The reconstruction included photos of bullet holes and marks.

The potential trajectory of the bullets was also highlighted.

Before the video was shown, justice Natalie Adams said it was the crown case that Baird was shot at close range but the defence argued he was shot from further away.

The judge warned the kitchen was not shown to scale and that not all the evidence relevant to the angle or distance of the shot to Baird’s head had been adduced.

The NSW police firearms examiner, Lucas Van Der Walt, said he was more certain of the trajectory of the bullet through the bedroom door because it had passed through 35mm thick wood.

Van Der Walt told the court that “stippling” had been found on the door around a bullet hole that the prosecution alleged was covered with putty and a plastic hook.

Stippling is the pattern made by gun shot propellant particles. The closer a target is to a barrel, the smaller the spread pattern would be, Van Der Walt said on Wednesday.

“[It] is going to pepper itself into that softer surface – in this case a painted door,” he told the jury.

The court was shown a video of police taking the door from Baird’s bedroom and shooting it with the same gun and ammunition that was allegedly used by Lamarre-Condon.

The pictures of both the original and test bullet hole were compared and shown to the jury. Van Der Walt said there was a “very similar spread pattern of the propellant particles impacting with the paint and the wood in the door”.

He suggested the muzzle of the firearm was 10 to 20cm away from Davies when it was discharged.

On the side of the door the bullet would have exited, he noted the splintering looked more opaque in the original hole, but he said that was because wood putty had been used to fill the hole.

Defence lawyer John Stratton SC suggested the bullet hole could have been created if there was a body in front of the door, but Van Der Walt said the “clear stippling” would prevent that scenario.

Asked why there was no other bullet marks or bullets found in the room, the expert said it could have hypothetically hit a pillow, jacket or similar item.

“If that bullet continued and penetrated any of these surfaces and that object was removed and discarded, we’ll never find that bullet,” he told the court.

Bullets shot in this way fell to the ground, he said, and given the scene had been cleaned extensively, a casing could have been picked up by cleaners, Van Der Walt told the jury.

The trial before justice Adams continues.

articles.title: Judge extends White House access to banned media outlets CNN, MS Now and Politico
articles.excerpt:
District court judge Timothy Kelly was ruling after the Trump administration blocked access to the three outlets in September

A federal judge ordered the White House on Tuesday to continue allowing j...
articles.body_text:
District court judge Timothy Kelly was ruling after the Trump administration blocked access to the three outlets in September

A federal judge ordered the White House on Tuesday to continue allowing journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico to access the building as the media coalition’s lawsuit against the Trump administration plays out.

Timothy Kelly, a district court judge, had on 24 September granted a 14-day reprieve for the news organizations, which six days earlier had been banned by the president in an extraordinary move from entering the White House grounds “as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS”.

“Defendants (except for President Trump) and their agents, representatives, and all persons or entities acting in concert with them, shall not execute, implement, or enforce the September 18, 2026, decision to revoke the White House ‘hard pass’ press credentials held by employees of CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO, thereby maintaining the status quo since the Court’s entry of a temporary restraining order on September 24, 2026,” the judge wrote in granting a preliminary injunction requested by the plaintiffs.

The organizations filed a lawsuit on 21 September seeking to overturn the ban as a violation of their rights under the US constitution. But that temporary restraining order expired on Tuesday, bringing the media companies into court late last week to ask for a preliminary injunction that would lift the ban during the duration of the lawsuit, which could take months.

During arguments at the E Barrett Prettyman Federal Courthouse in Washington, Kelly seemed inclined to lift the ban indefinitely, telling a lawyer for the federal government that his side had “a notice problem” that was “probably the biggest hurdle” they had to overcome.

The Trump White House gave no advance notice to the media companies affected to say that they were at risk of losing their press badges, which the news organizations have said are essential to their ability to cover the administration. While the White House sent letters to the media companies informing them of the ban, they did so post-hoc, after building access had already been cut off, in violation of binding court precedent.

In his ruling on Tuesday, Judge Kelly wrote that the plaintiffs “are likely to succeed not only on their due process claim, but also on their two First Amendment claims”. While access to the White House is not guaranteed, court precedent dictates that once it is provided to journalists, it cannot be taken away for editorial or viewpoint-based reasons.

During arguments for a preliminary injunction on 8 October, media lawyer Theodore J Boutrous told the judge that Trump had offered a “confession” – in a Time magazine interview last week – that he was banning the media companies explicitly because of the content of their reporting, not because of any other considerations, such as national security.

“The case has gotten stronger for the plaintiffs thanks to President Trump,” Boutrous told the judge.

The judge seemed to agree. “President Trump’s own comments suggest that he intended the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes to alter their reporting on him, bolstering the case that his action here is sufficient to deter a reporter of ordinary firmness from reporting in the same way she had before,” he wrote.

Although the White House has largely adhered to the judge’s prior ruling restoring access on a temporary basis, journalists for CNN and Politico have on occasion been prevented from performing “pool duty” – covering the daily activities of the president – because the administration has interpreted the judge’s temporary restraining order to solely require access to the White House complex, not smaller spaces like Air Force One or the Oval Office.

The judge required the media plaintiffs to post a bond of $1.

In a statement, Boutrous said of the judge’s ruling: “When the President issued his ‘ban on the free press,’ he blatantly and explicitly violated due process and the First Amendment. Since then, the President has repeatedly, candidly, and consistently admitted in public that he banned our clients from the White House to punish reporting he doesn’t like and to try to force journalists to cover him in ways he prefers.”

The court, he added, “was right to enjoin the White House from enforcing this ‘unconstitutional ban on the free press’ for the foreseeable future”.

articles.title: China and North Korea to open New Yalu River Bridge, state media reports
articles.excerpt:
China and North Korea will officially open the New Yalu River Bridge to traffic on Thursday, China’s state-run Xinhua news agency reports.

China completed its side of the bridge in 2014, hoping to bo...
articles.body_text:
China and North Korea will officially open the New Yalu River Bridge to traffic on Thursday, China’s state-run Xinhua news agency reports.

China completed its side of the bridge in 2014, hoping to boost trade ties. However, North Korea left its side unfinished for years as relations soured after Beijing supported United Nations sanctions over Pyongyang’s nuclear tests.

The first bridge connecting Russia and North Korea also opened earlier this month.

China’s exports to North Korea rose to a six-year high of $2.3bn last year, a 25 percent increase from the previous year. Chinese President Xi Jinping was welcomed in Pyongyang in June for the first time since 2019.

Since 2018, Beijing has tried to repair ties with Pyongyang, which also briefly began improving relations with Washington around the same time.

The China-North Korea relationship was forged during the Korean War. In 1961, the two countries signed the Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation and Mutual Assistance, which remains China’s only formal military alliance.

The treaty contains a mutual defence clause committing either side to assist the other if one comes under armed attack.

Although China was North Korea’s main diplomatic partner and protector for decades, relations strained after Beijing in 2017 supported tightening sanctions on Pyongyang for its nuclear weapons programme.

Analysts say North Korea’s recent growing relationship with Russia may have changed the balance of Pyongyang’s diplomatic dependence, reducing its reliance on Beijing.

North Korea and Russia signed a comprehensive strategic partnership treaty in 2024, including a mutual defence provision. Military and political ties between the two countries have grown considerably stronger, with North Korea deploying thousands of troops to fight in Russia’s war on Ukraine.

United States President Donald Trump also signalled an interest in repairing relations with Pyongyang last month, after his talks with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un abruptly ended in 2019. In his second term, Trump has floated meeting Kim again, though no official meeting has been set.

North Korea has not yet resumed issuing tourism visas to Chinese citizens, who once made up the bulk of its overseas visitors.

While North Korea’s trade with Russia largely involves military supplies, exchanges with China could arguably involve goods North Korea needs to develop its civilian economy, analysts have said.

articles.title: Singapore’s economy grows more than 5 percent amid AI boom
articles.excerpt:
Singapore’s economy grew more than 5 percent in the most recent quarter, continuing an AI-fuelled boom that has made the city-state one of the fastest-growing advanced economies.

Gross domestic produ...
articles.body_text:
Singapore’s economy grew more than 5 percent in the most recent quarter, continuing an AI-fuelled boom that has made the city-state one of the fastest-growing advanced economies.

Gross domestic product (GDP) grew 5.4 percent year-on-year between July and September, down from a 6.2 percent expansion in the second quarter, according to advance government estimates released on Wednesday.

Manufacturing, which is dominated by the city-state’s semiconductor industry, grew 7.5 percent, according to the estimates from the Ministry of Trade and Industry.

Increased output in “electronics, precision engineering, transport engineering and general manufacturing clusters” drove growth, the ministry said, offsetting declines in the chemicals and biomedical sectors.

Construction, including AI-related investments such as data centres, expanded 8.8 per cent, according to the figures.

Despite the heady expansion, Singapore’s central bank left its monetary policy settings untouched in its latest announcement on Wednesday, citing expectations that AI demand will cool in 2027.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore, which manages monetary policy through currency exchange rates rather than interest rates, said it expected core inflation to average 1.5–2.0 percent in 2026.

“Global AI-driven growth is expected to ease in the latter half of next year from its current exceptional pace, while higher interest rates, amid elevated inflation in the advanced economies, would weigh on final demand growth,” the central bank said in a statement.

Singapore is a major global player in the booming chip sector, a position that has helped it weather choppy economic conditions, including the energy shock prompted by the US-Israel war on Iran.

The Southeast Asian city-state accounts for roughly 10 percent of global semiconductor output and 20 percent of semiconductor equipment production, according to government figures.

Yeow Hwee Chua, an assistant professor of economics at Nanyang Technological University, described Singapore’s economic performance as “impressive for a high-income economy, especially given the uncertain global environment”.

“The global technology investment boom has been an important driver,” Chua told Al Jazeera.

“Strong demand for electronics has supported manufacturing and related wholesale trade, illustrating how Singapore benefits from its position in global supply chains,” he said.

Singapore’s economy is expected to grow 5 percent in 2026, according to the IMF’s latest economic forecast, faster than any other advanced economy except Taiwan.

The city-state’s GDP grew 5 percent in 2025, its second straight year of growth above 5 percent – the first such streak since 2010 and 2011.

articles.title: $20m public liability insurance to rally in a park: how council red tape hinders the right to protest
articles.excerpt:
Public gatherings stymied by bureaucracy, Australian Democracy Network and Deakin University researchers find

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Council red tape is stymiein...
articles.body_text:
Public gatherings stymied by bureaucracy, Australian Democracy Network and Deakin University researchers find

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Council red tape is stymieing the right to protest, a report has said, after a regional New South Wales council told a protest organiser they needed a $20m public liability insurance policy to hold a rally in a park.

A report released on Wednesday, co-authored by Australian Democracy Network (ADN) and Deakin University’s Centre for Law as Protection, raised concerns about incidents in which councils have required protest organisers to obtain insurance when rallies are held on council land. 
 It also expressed concern about the power some regional and urban councils have to issue financial penalties if public gatherings are held without a council permit.

In July, Mariella Gussoni notified Bathurst regional council she was holding a protest in a local park against the culling of brumbies in Kosciuszko national park. In her email to the council, seen by Guardian Australia, she said the protest would be part of nationwide rallies on a set day in August. The protest would include speakers and music, and she wasn’t sure if five or 50 people would attend, she wrote. 
 The council responded by letter, seen by Guardian Australia, saying it would permit her to hold her planned protest on the condition she take out a $20m public liability insurance policy, noting the council would not be liable for any loss or injury.

Nervous about what that could mean, and how much it would cost, the 61-year-old decided to hold the protest, which was attended by an estimated 120 people, next to the park. She notified police of her intention to hold the rally on the footpath – which is not council land – and said it went ahead without any issues.

“It scared me that I would be liable,” she said. “I had just let the council know as a courtesy.”

A spokesperson for Bathurst council said: “Council engaged with the event organisers at the time and won’t be providing any further comment on the matter.”

In Queanbeyan, organisers of a protest about the same issue which involved 16 horses and speeches in a park were also told they needed insurance, the ADN said. The organiser was initially quoted $5,000 for coverage that would include the use of horses, but the amount was reduced to $330 after securing participant waivers.

Report co-author and ADN protest rights campaigner, Anastasia Radievska, said council red tape such as insurance requirements could have a chilling effect on people speaking up about what’s happening in their local neighbourhoods.

“Often, community groups might spring up in relation to a specific local issue,” she said. “The more councils do this, the more other councils think that this is the way to interact with protest.”

The report said that across most Australian jurisdictions, “protest is unlawful or unprotected” without “permission from police, councils or place managers” and called for existing permit systems to be considered a process of notification rather than authorisation. It also recommended there be no insurance requirements.

NSW carries a $2,200 fine if a public gathering is held on council land without a permit, the report noted. This is a default requirement under the Local Government Act, but some councils have their own policies which deviate from the act. The city of Sydney has passed a number of motions affirming the right to protest on council land.

This requirement exists in addition to the police’s form 1 process, in which protesters can notify police of an intention to protest and gain immunity from being charged for offences such as obstructing a road in a designated area.

Tim Roberts, the president of the Council for Civil Liberties, said council demands for insurance or permits were “unhelpful” and a “reactionary approach”.

“It’s a blatant contravention of the right to protest,” Roberts said, referring to the implied right to freedom of political communication in the Australian constitution.

He agreed that protest organisers should only be required to give notice and not seek authorisation. He equated the council requiring insurance with calls for a user-pays system for the policing of protests.

Last week, a community group opposing a proposed $2.9bn datacentre on Sydney’s Cooks River was told by Bayside council it needed public liability insurance to hold a rally at Cahill Park in Wolli Creek. 
 The council also told the organisers it required an event application because their event included food, a film, and amplified sound. One of the organisers for Stop the Cooks River AI Project (SCRAP), Caitlin Boyce, said the council said it would need eight weeks to assess the application.

After receiving pro bono legal advice, the group decided to take their chances and go ahead with the protest without making an event application to the council. Boyce said she hasn’t heard from the council since going ahead with the rally.

A spokesperson for the Bayside council said it was not opposed to the public gathering, but the planned activities – which it said included a barbecue and smoking ceremony – “constitute an organised event and are subject to Council’s event approval requirements”.

Local Government NSW and the Office of Local Government were approached for comment.
